News outlets make choices about sources, language, images, and context. These decisions can reflect political views, commercial interests, or cultural assumptions. When audiences repeatedly encounter one perspective, they may accept it as complete or factual. This can deepen divisions and weaken trust in institutions. Bias does not always involve false information. A report may use accurate facts while omitting details that challenge its central message. Social media can amplify this effect because algorithms often promote content that attracts strong reactions. Users may then see fewer viewpoints and become more certain of their beliefs. Public opinion is also affected by the speed of online sharing. Headlines travel widely even when readers do not open the full article. Critical media literacy offers a response. People can compare coverage across outlets, check original sources, and separate evidence from commentary. Journalists also have a responsibility to disclose uncertainty and include relevant perspectives. A more balanced media environment will not eliminate disagreement but can help citizens debate with greater knowledge and fairness. Informed audiences are less easily misled.
